axes-points: A graph has two labeled axes: the horizontal axis (x) and the vertical axis (y). On a market graph, quantity goes on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical. Each row of a table becomes an ordered pair (horizontal value, vertical value), and you read a point by dropping lines to both axes. Points that rise to the right show a direct relationship; points that fall to the right show an inverse one.
slopes-curves: Slope measures how steeply a line rises or falls: the rise (vertical change) divided by the run (horizontal change). A positive slope rises to the right, a negative slope falls to the right, and a horizontal line has a slope of 0. A straight line keeps one slope; a curve changes slope as you move along it. A U-shaped curve has a negative slope, then a slope of 0 at its minimum point, then a positive slope.
shifts-movements: A curve on a market graph shows how quantity relates to price with everything else held equal. When the good's own price changes, the market moves along the same curve to a new point. When anything else changes, such as buyers' incomes, sellers' costs or the number of buyers, the whole curve shifts: right for a larger quantity at every price, left for a smaller one. Show a shift with the old curve labeled 1, the new curve labeled 2 and an arrow between them.
curves-crossing: Where a downward curve and an upward curve cross, one price and one quantity lie on both curves: the intersection. Read it with dashed lines to both axes. When one curve shifts, the crossing point slides along the other curve, and you compare the old and new points to say what happened to price and quantity. Areas on graphs are rectangles (base × height) and triangles (½ × base × height), with the base read on the horizontal axis and the height on the vertical axis.
scarcity: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are not, so every choice involves a trade-off. The resources used to make goods and services are the factors of production: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next-best alternative you give up, only the next best, and it includes time and other things that are not paid for in money.
economic-systems: Scarcity forces every society to decide what to produce, how and for whom. A market economy leaves those choices to households and firms and lets prices coordinate them; a command economy gives them to a central authority that coordinates by plans and orders; a mixed economy, the kind every real country has, combines markets with government rules, taxes and services. Markets work through institutions such as property rights, contracts and the rule of law, which give people incentives to produce and trade.
production-possibilities: A production possibilities curve shows every combination of two goods a producer can make when it uses all its resources efficiently with its current methods. Points on it are efficient, points inside waste resources, and points outside are out of reach for now. Moving along the curve shows the trade-off; the opportunity cost of one good is the amount of the other given up per unit gained. A bowed-out curve shows increasing opportunity cost, a straight one constant cost. More resources and better technology shift the curve out (growth).
comparative-advantage: Absolute advantage is making more of a good with the same resources; comparative advantage is making it at a lower opportunity cost. When producers specialize in the goods where they have a comparative advantage and trade, total output rises and both can consume combinations outside their own PPCs. Trade helps both when the terms of trade lie between the two producers' opportunity costs. From an output table, divide the other good given up by the good gained; from an input table, divide the hours for the good by the hours for the other good.
cost-benefit: A choice's total cost includes explicit costs, the money you pay, and implicit costs, the value of your own time and resources that you give up. Its total benefit is the satisfaction it gives a consumer or the revenue it brings a firm. Net benefit is total benefit minus total cost, and the best choice is the one with the largest net benefit. Ignoring implicit costs, or chasing the largest total benefit instead of the largest net benefit, leads to the wrong choice.
marginal-analysis: Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost: keep going while the marginal benefit is at least the marginal cost. Consumers get utility from goods, and marginal utility usually diminishes as they consume more. With a budget, a consumer maximizes total utility by buying the next unit with the highest marginal utility per dollar until the budget is spent and MU ÷ P is equal across goods. Sunk costs are already paid whatever you choose, so they never change the best decision.
demand: Demand shows how much buyers want at each price. By the law of demand, a higher price lowers the quantity demanded, because of the substitution and income effects and diminishing marginal utility. A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve; a change in tastes, income, the prices of substitutes or complements, expectations or the number of buyers shifts the whole curve. Market demand adds every buyer's quantity at each price.
supply: Supply shows how much sellers offer at each price. By the law of supply, a higher price raises the quantity supplied, because a higher price covers the rising cost of producing more. A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the curve; a change in input prices, technology, the prices of other goods the seller could make, taxes or subsidies, expectations or the number of sellers shifts the whole curve. Market supply adds every seller's quantity at each price.
price-elasticity-demand: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded responds to a price change: the percent change in quantity over the percent change in price, read as an absolute value. Above 1 demand is elastic, below 1 inelastic, at 1 unit elastic. The total revenue test follows: with elastic demand a price rise lowers total revenue, with inelastic demand it raises it. Close substitutes, a large budget share and more time to adjust make demand more elastic.
price-elasticity-supply: The price elasticity of supply is the percent change in quantity supplied divided by the percent change in price. Above 1 supply is elastic, below 1 inelastic; a vertical supply curve is perfectly inelastic and a horizontal one perfectly elastic. Supply is more elastic when sellers have spare capacity, easy access to inputs, goods they can store and more time to adjust. The more elastic supply is, the more a rise in demand shows up as more output rather than a higher price.
other-elasticities: Income elasticity of demand divides the percent change in quantity demanded by the percent change in income; cross-price elasticity divides the percent change in quantity demanded of one good by the percent change in the price of another. Unlike price elasticity of demand, both keep their sign. A positive income elasticity marks a normal good and a negative one an inferior good. A positive cross-price elasticity marks substitutes, a negative one complements, and one near zero unrelated goods.
equilibrium-surplus: A market is in equilibrium at the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Consumer surplus is the gain to buyers, the area under demand above the price; producer surplus is the gain to sellers, the area above supply below the price; both run out to the quantity traded. Their sum, total surplus, is largest at the competitive equilibrium, and prices act as signals that move resources to where buyers value them most.
disequilibrium-changes: At any price other than equilibrium the market is in disequilibrium: below it a shortage pushes the price up, above it a surplus pushes it down, until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. When one curve shifts, the equilibrium moves along the other: demand shifts move price and quantity together, supply shifts move them apart. When both shift, one change is certain and the other is indeterminate. Each shift also changes consumer, producer and total surplus, and elasticities decide how much of the change is in price.
government-intervention: Price ceilings, price floors, quotas, taxes and subsidies change the price signals and the quantity traded. A binding ceiling (below equilibrium) causes a shortage; a binding floor (above it) a surplus; in both, fewer units are traded. A per-unit tax shifts supply up, raises the price buyers pay, lowers the price sellers keep and raises revenue equal to the tax times the new quantity; a subsidy does the reverse at a cost of the subsidy times the new quantity. In a market that was efficient, each of these creates a deadweight loss, and the burden of a tax falls more on the less elastic side.
trade-policy: When a small country opens to trade, its price moves to the world price. If the world price is lower, it imports the gap between quantity demanded and domestic quantity supplied; consumers gain more than producers lose. If it is higher, the country exports and producers gain more than consumers lose. Either way total surplus rises. A tariff raises the domestic price, increases domestic output, cuts imports, raises revenue equal to the tariff times the remaining imports, and creates two deadweight loss triangles. An import quota has the same effect on quantities and price without the tariff revenue.
production-function: A production function shows how much output a firm gets from its inputs. In the short run at least one input is fixed, so adding workers eventually brings diminishing marginal returns: each worker adds less than the one before. Marginal product is the change in total product divided by the change in labor, and average product is total product divided by labor. Marginal product above average pulls the average up; below it, the average falls; total product peaks where marginal product reaches zero.
short-run-costs: Short-run costs are fixed (the same at every output, even zero) or variable (rising with output); total cost is their sum. Dividing by output gives AFC, AVC and ATC. Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output; diminishing marginal returns make it rise. Because MC pulls an average down when below it and up when above it, MC crosses AVC and ATC at their lowest points. A change in a fixed cost shifts only ATC; a change in a variable cost shifts MC, AVC and ATC.
long-run-costs: In the long run every input can change, so a firm chooses the plant size with the lowest cost for each output; long-run average total cost traces those lowest costs. Returns to scale compare the growth of output with the growth of all inputs. With input prices unchanged, increasing returns bring economies of scale (falling LRATC), constant returns a flat LRATC and decreasing returns diseconomies of scale (rising LRATC). Minimum efficient scale, the smallest output at the lowest LRATC, compared with market demand, helps decide how many firms an industry can hold.
types-of-profit: Accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs from total revenue. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, the income the owner gives up by using her own time, savings and property in the business, so it is never larger than accounting profit. Zero economic profit is a normal profit: the owner earns what she could earn elsewhere. Positive economic profit means resources earn more here than in their next-best use, which draws in new firms; an economic loss means they earn less.
profit-maximization: Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from one more unit. A firm maximizes profit by producing where MR = MC: from a table, the last unit whose MR is at least its MC. A firm that sells every unit at a market price it cannot change has MR = AR = P, so its demand curve is a horizontal line, d = MR = AR = P. Profit is TR - TC = (P - ATC) x q at the profit-maximizing output: on a graph, the rectangle from the price down to ATC, out to that output.
firm-decisions: In the short run a firm compares the price with average variable cost: if P is at least the lowest point of AVC it produces where MR = MC, even at a loss, because closing would lose the whole fixed cost; if P is below that point it shuts down. Fixed costs do not change that choice. Above the shutdown point, MC is the firm's short-run supply curve. In the long run, economic profit draws new firms in and losses push firms out; entry shifts market supply right and exit shifts it left, moving the price until economic profit is zero.
perfect-competition: In perfect competition, many firms sell an identical product and can enter or exit freely, so each firm is a price taker: its demand curve is horizontal at the market price, d = MR = AR = P. Drawn side by side, the market sets the price and the firm produces where MR = MC; profit or loss is (P - ATC) x q. In the long run, profit draws firms in and losses push firms out until the price equals minimum ATC: zero economic profit, P = MC (allocative efficiency) and production at the lowest ATC (productive efficiency). In a constant-cost industry the price returns to the same level, so long-run supply is horizontal.
imperfect-competition: Firms with market power are price makers: they face a downward-sloping demand curve, so they sell more only by cutting the price on every unit, and their marginal revenue curve lies below demand. They produce where MR = MC and read the price from demand, above marginal cost. Barriers to entry (legal rights, key resources, economies of scale) protect their profit from entry. Monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition differ in the number of sellers, how different their products are and how hard entry is.
monopoly: A monopolist produces where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve above that quantity. Its profit is (P minus ATC) times Q; it can last because barriers block entry. It produces less and charges more than a competitive industry would, on the elastic part of demand, leaving a deadweight loss between D and MC from its quantity to the efficient one. A natural monopoly, whose ATC falls over the whole range of demand, can be regulated at P = MC (efficient but a loss) or at the fair-return price P = ATC (zero economic profit). A lump-sum tax changes ATC and profit but not price or quantity.
price-discrimination: Price discrimination is charging different buyers different prices for the same good when costs do not differ. It needs market power, a way to sort buyers and a way to stop resale, and it charges the higher price to the less elastic group. It raises the firm's profit and usually its output. With perfect price discrimination, each buyer pays the most they will pay, so the MR curve is the demand curve and the firm produces where demand meets MC: the efficient quantity, with no deadweight loss and no consumer surplus.
monopolistic-competition: In monopolistic competition, many firms sell differentiated products and entry is easy. Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, produces where MR = MC and reads its price from demand, so in the short run it can earn a profit or make a loss. Profit draws entry and losses cause exit, shifting each firm's demand until it is tangent to ATC: zero economic profit. At that point price is above marginal cost and output is below the minimum of ATC (excess capacity), the cost of the variety buyers enjoy.
oligopoly-game-theory: In an oligopoly a few interdependent firms must consider each other's choices, which a payoff matrix shows. A best response is the strategy that pays a player most with the rival's choice held fixed. A dominant strategy is the best response to every choice of the rival, proved with both comparisons. A Nash equilibrium is a cell where each player is making its best response, so neither gains by switching alone; a game can have one, several or none. In a prisoner's dilemma, dominant strategies lead to a Nash equilibrium that is worse for both than the joint-profit cell, which is why collusion and cartels tend to break down. A tax, subsidy or cost change alters payoffs and can change the equilibrium.
factor-markets: Firms buy labor, land and capital in factor markets, and their demand for these inputs is derived from the demand for the products the inputs make. A worker is worth the extra revenue the worker brings in, the marginal revenue product: MRP = MP × MR, or MP × P for a price taker. MRP falls as workers are added because marginal product falls, and the MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labor. A higher product price or higher productivity raises MRP.
factor-demand-supply: A labor market works like any market, with the wage as its price. Labor demand shifts with the demand for the product, productivity and the prices of other inputs (substitutes lower it when they get cheaper; complements raise it), because each changes MRP or how firms combine inputs. Labor supply shifts with the number of qualified people, pay in other jobs and the appeal of the work. Then read the new wage and employment from the graph: a demand shift moves them the same way; a supply shift moves them in opposite ways.
competitive-factor-markets: In a perfectly competitive labor market the wage is set where market labor demand meets labor supply, and each firm is a wage taker facing a horizontal line S = MFC = W. A firm maximizes profit by hiring where MRP = MRC, which from a table is the last worker whose MRP is at least the wage. A higher wage means fewer workers, a higher product price or productivity means more, and a fixed cost changes nothing. To make any output at the least cost, the MP per dollar must be equal across inputs.
monopsony: A monopsony is the only buyer of a kind of labor. Because it must raise everyone's pay to hire one more worker, its MFC lies above labor supply. It hires where MRP = MFC and pays the wage read on the labor supply curve at that quantity, so it hires fewer workers and pays less than a competitive market would, with deadweight loss between MRP and labor supply. The wage bill is the wage times the workers hired. A minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage makes MFC flat and raises both the wage and employment.
market-efficiency: A quantity is socially efficient where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost: every unit worth more than it costs is made, and no other. Total surplus is largest there. A competitive market in which demand and supply reflect all benefits and costs reaches that point on its own. Taxes, subsidies, price controls and monopoly move the quantity away from it, and the lost net benefit is deadweight loss, a triangle between MSB and MSC that points toward the efficient quantity. A market outcome that is not efficient is a market failure.
externalities: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a market. With a negative externality, the social cost exceeds the private cost (or the social benefit falls short of the private benefit), so the market, which uses private curves, produces more than the efficient quantity where MSB = MSC; with a positive externality it produces less. The deadweight loss is the triangle between the social and private curves from the market quantity to the efficient quantity. A per-unit tax or subsidy equal to the external cost or benefit at the efficient quantity moves the market there; a lump-sum tax does not, because it leaves marginal cost unchanged.
public-goods: Goods differ in rivalry (does one person's use leave less for others?) and excludability (can nonpayers be kept out?). Private goods are rival and excludable and markets handle them well. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable: people can free ride, so markets provide too little, even when the sum of everyone's benefit exceeds the cost, and governments often provide them with taxes. Common resources are rival but nonexcludable, so they are overused. Club goods are excludable but nonrival.
intervention-structures: The same policy can have different effects in different market structures. A price ceiling cuts output in a competitive market but can raise a monopoly's output by making its marginal revenue flat. Regulators of a natural monopoly choose between the socially optimal price (P = MC, efficient but with a loss that needs a subsidy) and the fair-return price (P = ATC, a normal profit). Lump-sum taxes and subsidies change only profit; per-unit ones change marginal cost and so output and price. A minimum wage lowers employment in a competitive labor market but can raise it in a monopsony.
inequality: The Lorenz curve shows how income is shared: the cumulative percentage of income held by the cumulative percentage of households, from poorest to richest. The diagonal line of equality means equal shares, and the further the curve bows below it, the more unequal the distribution. The Gini coefficient measures that gap as a share of the area under the line. Taxes are progressive, proportional or regressive by how their share of income changes with income, and progressive taxes and transfer payments move the after-tax Lorenz curve toward equality. Inequality comes from differences in skills, wealth, discrimination, market power and luck.
